Key Message 1...Mainly dry weather continues through Saturday.

NW'erly flow aloft affects Western and Central NY through
Saturday as a high pressure ridge at the surface and aloft
builds from the Canadian Prairies and vicinity. Primarily fair
weather is expected as stabilizing subsidence accompanies the
ridge. However, a prominent shortwave trough embedded in the 
flow aloft will traverse central Lake Ontario, the Genesee 
Valley, and points east in our CWA this afternoon through early 
evening. Isolated showers and thunderstorms are possible in the 
same areas and during the same time period as low-level 
convergence and moist ascent along a surface trough axis 
accompanying the shortwave trough and any downshear outflow 
boundaries interacting with sufficient low-level vertical wind 
shear release weak boundary layer CAPE amidst moderate to strong
deep-layer bulk shear. Similar to yesterday, a lack of greater 
instability should prevent storms from becoming severe.

Weather pattern evolution at the surface and aloft will result 
in negligible air mass change through Saturday. Daily highs in 
the 70's to lower 80's are expected today and Saturday. Mainly
clear to partly cloudy sky and weak surface winds should result
in lows reaching mainly the upper 40's to near 60F around 
daybreak today and Saturday, respectively. The coolest lows are
expected in Lewis County, especially the Black River Valley, 
where efficient radiational cooling should be complemented by 
cool air drainage from adjacent higher terrain. Sufficient 
radiational cooling and low-level moisture are expected to 
result in patchy radiation fog and localized steam fog in the 
river and lake valleys of the Western Southern Tier, Finger 
Lakes, and Eastern Lake Ontario Region during the predawn hours 
through shortly after daybreak today and Saturday, respectively.

Key Message 2...The potential for scattered showers and thunderstorms
increases this Saturday night into Sunday.

During Saturday night through Sunday morning, the above-mentioned
ridge at the surface and aloft should exit E'ward and be followed
by W'erly flow aloft and embedded shortwave troughs. Surface
weather pattern evolution is less certain, but latest trends in
more-reliable NWP models, including the ECMWF model, continue to
suggest a surface warm front will sweep NE'ward through our CWA
Saturday night through Sunday morning as a surface low wobbles
ESE'ward in vicinity of the northern Great Lakes. The warm 
front will usher-in a warmer and more humid air mass originating
over the Gulf. Moist isentropic ascent along the upper-reaches 
of the warm front and low-level convergence/moist ascent along 
the surface front should release enough CAPE, including elevated
CAPE, to generate periodic and scattered showers/thunderstorms,
especially Sunday morning. Lows should reach mainly the 50's to
mid 60's early Sunday morning before readings begin to moderate
before daybreak as low-level WAA strengthens ahead of and 
behind the surface warm front.

Lows should reach the 50's to mid 60's early Sunday morning 
before readings begin to moderate before daybreak as low-level 
WAA strengthens ahead of and behind the surface warm front.

Cyclonic W'erly to WNW'erly flow aloft and embedded shortwave
troughs should impact our region this Sunday afternoon through 
Monday. At the surface, the low may wobble ESE'ward from near 
the northern Great Lakes to near the Gulf of Maine, which should
allow a cold front to sweep E'ward through our CWA Sunday 
evening through Sunday night. Additional scattered showers and 
thunderstorms are expected along and ahead of the cold front, 
amidst weak to perhaps moderate instability and moderate to 
strong deep-layer bulk shear. Severe storms appear possible 
Sunday afternoon into the evening, but their occurrence will be 
contingent on multiple factors, including the degree of diurnal 
destabilization of the warm/moist sector boundary layer. Behind 
the cold front, a surface ridge attempts to build from the Upper
Midwest and vicinity through Monday. However, isolated rain 
showers remain possible since subtle shortwave troughs aloft and
attendant surface trough axes should traverse Western and 
Central NY generally from west to east. In addition, 850 mb 
temperatures cooling to near 10C over the ~23C to ~24C eastern 
Great Lakes and sufficient low-level moisture on the synoptic 
scale should allow isolated lake-effect rain showers to impact 
areas generally southeast of Lakes Erie and Ontario, amidst at 
least weak lake-induced instability and a NW'erly mean low-level
flow, overnight Sunday night into Monday morning.

High temperatures are forecast to reach the 70's to lower 80's
Sunday afternoon. Lows should reach mainly the upper 50's to 
mid 60's around daybreak Monday. Late afternoon highs should 
reach the 70's on Monday as a somewhat cooler air mass overspreads
the eastern Great Lakes, behind the cold front.
